images.title: Terracotta dreams
images.caption: Nice, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, France
images.desc: Bathed in a sun-kissed glow, Nice is a patchwork of terracotta rooftops, historic churches, and pastel façades along the French Riviera, as seen in today's image. Founded by ancient Greeks and long connected to the Italian royal House of Savoy, Nice officially became part of France in 1860. Today, that layered past remains visible throughout the coastal city in the south of France, where old-world architecture meets the blue Mediterranean waters and sunlit hills of the Côte d'Azur.

images.title: Feasting in the fjords
images.caption: Diving humpback whale, Kvaloya, Troms, Northern Norway
images.desc: Off the coast of Kvaløya in Troms, Northern Norway, humpback whales move through the cold Arctic waters in search of a proper feast. They visit this region during the winter months, following migrating herring into the fjords. Humpbacks are famous for bubble-net feeding, a remarkable hunting technique in which whales blow rings of bubbles to corral fish before lunging upward, open-mouthed, to catch their prey. In today's image, a humpback slips beneath the icy waves under a glowing pastel sky, capturing a moment of tranquility in Norway's wild north.

images.copyright: The "Body of Knowledge" sculpture by Jaume Plensa at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany (© Todamo/Shutterstock)
images.title: Where ideas take shape
images.caption: World Philosophy Day
images.desc: It's World Philosophy Day, when big thinkers gather to discuss life's eternal mysteries. To celebrate, today's image features the "Body of Knowledge" sculpture at Goethe University in Frankfurt, Germany, which molds steel letters from eight different alphabets into a human form. Spanish artist Jaume Plensa explains: "Our body is the home of the spirit. The place in which ideas live." On World Philosophy Day, we're all encouraged to look beyond easy answers and explore the questions that shape us, and the world around us.

images.copyright: Pair of barn owls (© Zahoor Salmi/Getty Images)
images.title: Hunting from dusk till dawn
images.caption: A pair of barn owls at dusk
images.desc: These barn owls, bathed in evening light, are waiting for the hunt to begin. As night falls, these birds of prey swoop into action, listening for tiny movements in grass or leaves made by mice and voles. Their heart-shaped faces help funnel sound into some of the sharpest ears in the animal kingdom. This allows them to locate their prey with pinpoint precision in the dark before swooping silently, their soft feathers muffling their approach. In autumn, young barn owls strike out to find their own territories. As the nights grow longer, you might spot them earlier in the evening, gliding over fields in search of supper.

images.copyright: Trail of the Cedars, Glacier National Park, Montana (© DBushue Photography/Getty Images)
images.title: Step into the great outdoors
images.caption: National Take a Hike Day
images.desc: Happy National Take a Hike Day! It's time to breathe in that crisp fall air and step into the great outdoors. Today's image features the Trail of the Cedars, one of 700 miles of hiking trails in Glacier National Park, Montana. Its 0.9-mile-long loop includes a raised boardwalk which cuts a path through western red cedars and hemlock trees. The park boasts routes for all abilities, taking in alpine lakes, wildflower meadows, mountain passes, and wilderness stretching to the Canadian border. But if you don't have spectacular scenery on your doorstep, a short stroll along a tree-lined street is an easy way to celebrate and enjoy the benefits of getting out, as the days draw in.

images.copyright: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument, New Mexico (© Chiara Salvadori/Getty Images)
images.title: Built to last
images.caption: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument anniversary
images.desc: Incredible views and rock-solid foundations are part of the charm of these ancient dwellings, set into the cliffside in New Mexico. Nomads had long used the natural caves above Cliff Dweller Creek as temporary shelter, but it was the Native American Mogollon people who made them their home. Archaeologists believe they created dozens of rooms inside five alcoves in the 1270s and 1280s. Up to 15 families lived here at any one time, raising children, making pottery, and overlooking the fertile Gila River valley where they grew crops and hunted wildlife. For reasons unknown, the Mogollon people moved on around 1300, leaving behind one of the American Southwest's most important archaeological sites. On November 16, 1907, President Theodore Roosevelt designated the area as Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument, helping to ensure its preservation for future generations.

images.copyright: Frozen azalea with red leaves (© avoferten/Shutterstock)
images.title: Frosty foliage
images.caption: Frost on azalea foliage
images.desc: As fall's first frost works its way across the South, ice crystals form on the leaves of evergreen shrubs, like this azalea. Long gone are the pinks, oranges, and yellows of their spring blooms, but a new colorful display awaits, as their green leaves turn shades of red and purple. For the plants, the new pigments protect their leaves as temperatures drop, but for gardeners, they create a vibrant autumnal display, framed in white frost. When spring arrives, new growth will restore the shrub's green leaves, and the colorful cycle begins anew.

images.copyright: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China (© Juan Romero/Cavan Images)
images.title: The only way is up
images.caption: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China
images.desc: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to the world's largest collection of skyscrapers. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters allowed the island to develop as a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk, and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth rocketed in the decades after World War II, fueling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbor and the hills, developers had to build upward, creating this distinctive skyline. In 2026, Hong Kong has 569 buildings above 492 feet high—more than any other city.
